# Examining artificial intelligence literacy among pre-service teachers for future classrooms 

### Musa Adekunle Ayanwale [a,\*, Owolabi Paul Adelana](#computers-and-education-open) [b, Rethabile Rosemary Molefi](#computers-and-education-open) [c, ](#computers-and-education-open)Olalekan Adeeko [d, Adebayo Monsur Ishola](#computers-and-education-open) [e ](#computers-and-education-open)

a _Department of Science and Technology Education, University of Johannesburg, South Africa_ b _Institute of Educational Technology (IET), The Open University, United Kingdom_ 

c _Department of Languages and Social Education, Faculty of Education, National University of Lesotho, Lesotho_ d _Department of Computer Science, Faculty of Science, National Open University of Nigeria, Nigeria_ 

e _Department of Educational Technology, College of Specialized and Professional Education, Tai Solarin University of Education, Nigeria_ 

ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT 

_Keywords:_ In the context of global integration and increasing reliance on Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education, evaluating AI literacy the AI literacy of pre-service teachers is crucial. As future architects of educational systems, pre-service teachers AI emotion regulation must not only possess pedagogical expertise but also a strong foundation in AI literacy. This quantitative study Knowing and understanding AI 

examines AI literacy among 529 pre-service teachers in a Nigerian university, utilizing structural equation 

Detect AI Pre-service teachers modeling (SEM) for comprehensive analysis. The research explores various dimensions of AI literacy, revealing 

that a profound understanding of AI significantly predicts positive outcomes in AI use, detection, ethics, creation, and problem-solving. However, no correlation exists between AI knowledge and emotion regulation or the assumption that active AI use enhances AI detection capabilities. The study identifies a trade-off between AI application and creation, emphasizing the ethical considerations intertwined with emotional and persuasive facets of AI use. It also supports the link between AI creation and problem-solving, emphasizing the foundational role of AI knowledge in shaping diverse aspects of AI literacy among pre-service teachers. The findings offer valuable insights for educators, administrators, policymakers, and researchers aiming to enhance AI literacy in 

pre-service teacher education programs.

world \[[3\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). The increasing reliance on AI technologies in education is evident not only in the proliferation of smart classrooms and adaptive learning systems but also in the demand for educators with a nuanced understanding of AI’s capabilities, limitations, and ethics. As AI gains prominence in education globally, it becomes imperative to assess the AI literacy of pre-service teachers, who represent the future architects of educational systems. Essentially, the transformation brought about by AI in education underscores the importance of educators possessing not only pedagogical skills but also a solid foundation in AI literacy. According to Kandlhofer et al. \[[9\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence), the term "AI literacy" was initially defined until 2016 as the ability to understand the basic techniques and concepts behind AI products. Definitions of AI literacy vary in terms of the number and configuration of competencies, resulting in multiple conceptualizations of the term. AI literacy encompasses competencies that enable individuals to critically evaluate AI technologies, commu- nicate and collaborate effectively with AI, and use AI as a tool in various settings such as online, at home and in the workplace \[[10\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Additionally, it is defined as a bundle of four core capabilities: technology-related, work-related, human-machine-related, and learning-related capabil- ities \[[11\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Cetindamar et al. argue that technological capabilities, including tools and data literacy, are necessary for AI literacy, but in-depth programming skills are not included. Other conceptualizations, such as, emphasize components like awareness, usage, evaluation, and ethics, without including the ability to develop AI applications. Zhang et al. \[[12\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence) propose AI literacy components, including factual knowledge, ethical and societal implications, and AI career future, but exclude in-depth technical knowledge about AI creation. 

Fundamentally, comprehension of artificial intelligence (AI) re- volves around AI concepts, skills, knowledge, and attitudes that do not necessitate prior familiarity. Rather than being mere end-users of AI applications, students should grasp its technologies and operational principles, especially as AI learning tools (e.g., teachable machines, ro- botics) become more age-appropriate for student implementation of machine learning models Ng et al. \[[5\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Researchers have developed learning curricula and hands-on activities fostering AI literacy, focusing on how students acquire AI concepts \[[13,14\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence), including learning AI through interaction with AI agents and robotics, and via AI-driven technologies such as simulation (e.g., Teachable Machine) and draw- ing tools (e.g., image stylizer). These opportunities enable students to interact, experience, and explore AI \[[14\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Once a solid understanding of AI concepts is attained, the subsequent cognitive level involves the use and application of AI, employing AI concepts and applications in various contexts \[[13,15\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Ethical use of AI concepts and applications is also crucial for societal well-being. The ability to leverage AI thinking through data analytics and interpret findings from machine-learned discovery of hidden patterns in data applies at this second level of AI literacy \[[16\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). 

At the third cognitive level of AI literacy, students can evaluate and create AI. Beyond knowing and using AI concepts and practices, studies have extended AI literacy to competencies enabling students to critically evaluate AI technologies, communicate effectively with AI, and create AI-driven artifacts \[[10\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). For instance, students have participated in co-creating AI-driven installations in public areas and museums to develop their AI literacy and experiences, enhancing scientific and technological knowledge applied in research-based learning to address practical problems (Long et al., 2019; \[[17\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence)). The final cognitive level of AI literacy, according to Ng et al. \[[18,19\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence), is AI ethics. As AI significantly influences day-to-day decision-making, misused or poorly designed AI could cause irreparable harm to humans and society \[[20\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Ethical con- siderations, such as bias in AI, legal responsibility, and intellectual property, are essential, highlighting the need for safety and ethical guidelines in using and designing AI technologies \[[21\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Human-centered and ethical considerations in AI education are increasingly pertinent to cultivate socially responsible designers, users, and evaluators of AI technologies Ng et al. \[[5,15,22\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence)). 

As AI emerges as a crucial technological skill in the twenty-first 

century, pre-service teachers, especially those in the formative stages of their teaching portfolios, need to integrate AI and literacy to equip students with essential abilities for navigating the digital world through AI-driven technologies Ng et al. \[[5,23\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence)). AI literacy for pre-service teachers is pivotal in preparing them for the challenges and opportu- nities ahead, ensuring they can effectively leverage AI tools in the classroom to foster innovation, collaboration, and personalized learning experiences. AI-literate teachers serve as role models, promoting tech- nological fluency and adaptability. Despite the growing integration of AI in education, there exists a notable gap in the understanding of AI lit- eracy among pre-service teachers, particularly in the context of Nigeria. The educational landscape is evolving rapidly, with face-to-face class- room activities giving way to modern strategies fueled by ICT \[[24,25\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Many teacher preparation programs in Nigeria have yet to fully incor- porate AI-related content into their curricula, leaving future educators ill-prepared for the AI-driven educational landscape. The lack of expo- sure to AI concepts, ethical considerations, and practical applications impedes pre-service teachers’ ability to harness the potential benefits of AI in their future classrooms. Our observations reveal a general dearth of empirical studies documenting pre-service teachers’ AI literacy in the Nigerian context, contrasting with numerous studies on AI literacy among teachers globally. Inadequate AI literacy among pre-service teachers has consequences beyond individual educators, affecting the broader education system. Teachers lacking AI literacy may struggle to integrate AI tools effectively, missing opportunities for personalized instruction, data-driven decision-making, and improved educational outcomes. Addressing shortfalls in AI literacy among pre-service teachers requires a thorough examination of AI literacy, holding pro- found significance for the future of education in Nigeria and beyond. This study is also significant because taking teachers’ (especially trainee teachers’) perspectives into consideration when creating AI education programmes especially in the context of secondary schools is very important \[[26,27\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Education’s transformative potential relies on empowered teachers, as they shape the next generation’s ability to thrive in a technology-driven world. Understanding pre-service teach- ers’ AI literacy identifies gaps in current teacher preparation programs, informing necessary adjustments to better equip them for the evolving demands of the educational landscape. 

This paper aims to contribute to the existing knowledge on AI liter- acy among pre-service teachers in Nigeria and beyond, offering insights into the current landscape and proposing a framework for integrating AI education into teacher preparation programs. By exploring AI literacy among pre-service teachers, this study seeks to bridge the gap and promote a comprehensive understanding of AI’s role in education, encompassing both technical aspects and ethical considerations. The findings hold potential for transformative educational experiences that leverage AI to foster innovation, equity, and student success. The paper is structured as follows: [Section 1 ](#computers-and-education-open)provides an introduction, Section 2 presents a detailed literature review, Section 3 outlines the methodol- ogy, Section 4 presents and interprets the results, and Section 5 discusses the implications of the findings. Sub-Sections 5.1 and 5.2 address the practical implications of the results and limitations, and future work. Finally, [Section 6 ](#tions-it-is-recommended-that-future-research-endeavors-aim-to-address-these-gaps-and-build-upon-the-current-findings-this-approach-will-statements-on-open-data-and-ethics)concludes the study. 

2\. **Literature review** 

_2.1._ _Artificial intelligence in education_ 

In the era of the fourth industrial revolution (4IR), smart technolo- gies and information and communication technology (ICT) are playing increasingly important roles in various aspects of human life (Ishola et al., 2022). Among these technologies, artificial intelligence (AI) stands out as a powerful tool that has the potential to reshape many areas of society within the rapidly evolving technological landscape. One domain that stands to benefit significantly from AI is education, commonly known as AI in education \[[28\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). This involves using machine 

learning algorithms, data analysis, and other AI techniques to enhance different elements of the educational process. The overall goal of AI in education is to create more personalized, efficient, and effective learning environments \[[29,30\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). AI has been applied to teaching, administrative procedures, curriculum development, instruction, and student learning processes \[[31,32\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Through automation, AI has notably increased the efficiency of administrative tasks such as assessing students’ work, grading, and providing feedback on assignments \[[31\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). 

A significant contribution of AI in education lies in its ability to personalize learning experiences according to individual needs \[[33\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Unlike traditional educational approaches, which often adopt a one-size-fits-all model and may not cater to diverse learning styles and paces \[[30\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence), AI algorithms can create customized learning paths by analyzing student data, identifying strengths and weaknesses, and adjusting content accordingly. This approach ensures a more engaging learning experience, maximizing educational effectiveness by address- ing each student’s needs. Intelligent tutoring systems powered by AI are transformative, as they assess student performance, identify areas for improvement, offer tailored feedback, and provide an interactive and adaptive learning environment \[[34\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Moreover, using AI in education is expected to enhance individualized learning experiences, facilitate effective learning encounters, nurture students’ creativity, and alleviate the burden on teachers \[[33\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). The literature suggests that AI has the potential to support special education needs, cater to diverse learning styles, serve as a learning mentor, enhance the efficiency of the learning process, and guide students in developing career plans \[[35,36\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Despite the significant promise of integrating AI into education, there are challenges. Concerns about data privacy arise, as AI often in- volves collecting and processing sensitive student data \[[34\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Moreover, relying on AI for individualized learning may risk diminishing the human touch and emotional understanding in the teacher-student relationship \[[30,37\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Additionally, there is a potential for perpetuating existing inequalities, given the digital divide, where not all students have equal access to the technology required for AI-driven education \[[38\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). While automated grading systems are efficient, they may not fully capture the subtle and creative aspects of student work, undervaluing specific skills. Ethical concerns about the transparency and account- ability of decision-making systems in AI education also emerge, as algorithmic bias may lead to unequal outcomes for students \[[37\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Finally, the rapid pace of technological advancements may outpace educational institutions’ ability to adapt, posing challenges for in- structors regarding training and keeping up with new AI technologies \[[39\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Therefore, it is crucial to strike a careful balance between the benefits of AI and these challenges for the responsible and equitable integration of AI into the educational landscape. 

_2.2._ _Artificial intelligence in African education_ 

Before discussing AI in African education, it’s important to define what African education is. African education focuses on the individual and the community, emphasizing practicality, relevance, and real-life experiences. It also values culture, tradition, and spirituality, taking a hands-on and experiential approach compared to Western education systems. African education sees technology as a tool to enhance the quality of life for individuals and communities. However, Africa faces challenges in implementing technology due to a lack of resources and infrastructure. Despite this, many African teachers believe that tech- nology can bridge gaps between rural and urban areas and socioeco- nomic groups \[[40\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). AI is an evolving technology that has the potential to reshape education in Africa. It can revolutionize learning processes, making education more accessible for all. AI in African education in- cludes methods such as AI-driven conversational agents that provide personalized mentoring and AI-powered platforms that offer tailored learning experiences. AI also automates functions like evaluating homework, allowing teachers to focus on important matters. Additionally, AI can address unique challenges in African education 

by providing educational content in indigenous languages. Overall, AI can have a significant positive impact on education in Africa by providing customized learning experiences, improving efficiency, and addressing specific challenges faced by educational systems on the continent. The utilization of remote learning platforms and virtual classrooms in Africa allows educational systems to leverage AI, over- coming geographical barriers and ensuring equal access to high-quality education. This democratization of education enables individuals from underserved communities to pursue academic goals and uplift their communities. It is important to recognize that AI not only transforms how children learn but also empowers teachers in their roles \[[41\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). AI-powered grading systems save educators time, allowing them to focus on individualized instruction and provide timely feedback. Addi- tionally, AI systems can analyze teaching approaches and offer tailored professional development programs, enhancing teachers’ skills and effectiveness in the classroom. One challenge in African education is the early detection of learning problems in children. AI-driven algorithms can examine student performance patterns and behaviors, enabling the early identification of potential learning problems. This early interven- tion ensures that educators and parents can provide timely support, leading to greater academic success for all students. Notably, the 2020 Global Government Artificial Intelligence Preparation Index raised concerns about Africa’s low AI preparation scores, emphasizing the need for increased AI research and development activities on the continent. Despite efforts to bridge the gap, there is a scarcity of literature on AI in Africa, highlighting the necessity for more research to understand the specific challenges and opportunities in adopting AI technologies. Several studies in Africa have focused on AI in education. For instance, Oyelere et al. \[42\] evaluated AI in African schools, suggesting the con- textualization of materials for effective teaching and learning. Ayanwale \[43\] researched secondary school students’ intentions to learn AI, finding that many learners have a favorable attitude toward AI and are confident in their ability to learn it. Sanusi et al. \[44\] explored learners’ AI education competencies in an African K-12 setting, emphasizing the need for activities promoting collaboration in the AI curriculum. Other research has examined the application of AI in education in Nigerian universities \[45\] and compulsory education in Namibia, highlighting factors influencing teachers’ intention to teach AI \[46\]. Notably, there is a significant gap in the literature concerning studies on pre-service teachers’ AI literacy, making Nigeria an intriguing area for explora- tion. Consequently, this research aims to examine the AI literacy of pre-service teachers in Nigeria. 

_2.3._ _Pre-service teachers’ AI literacy_ 

AI literacy is now recognized as a crucial skill set imperative for individuals in the current era of intelligence. Traditionally, literacy has been defined as the ability to comprehend written language and artic- ulate thoughts in written form \[[10\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). This term has expanded to encompass various literacy forms, such as media literacy, digital liter- acy, information literacy, computer literacy, and AI literacy \[[10,](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence)47\]. Individuals equipped with these skills can adeptly utilize technology and computers to acquire new knowledge and skills alongside their peers in contemporary times \[48,49\]. Therefore, Long and Magerko \[[10\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence) define AI literacy as a combination of abilities that empower individuals to critically analyze AI technologies, engage in productive communication and collaboration with AI, and make effective use of AI as a tool in diverse settings including online platforms, home environments, and professional workplaces. In the twenty-first century, AI emerges as a pivotal technological skill, giving rise to the concept of AI literacy. AI literacy pertains to the essential skills individuals need to thrive, learn, and work in the digital realm through AI-powered technologies \[[23\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Initially confined to university computer science departments, AI edu- cation faced challenges in providing adequate support to K-12 children due to the demand for advanced programming skills. However, recent advancements in age-appropriate software and technological devices 

have enabled pre-service teachers to enhance the learning experience for younger students. This implies that there is more need for the pre-service teachers to know and understand AI literacy to leverage it in their future classroom teaching and learning. 

There is limited research on pre-service teachers’ AI literacy, most of the research concentrates on in-service teachers AI literacy. Hence the main objective of this study is to examine pre-service teachers AI literacy in Nigerian context. Scholars such as Brundage et al. \[50\] depict that the widespread integration of various technologies, such as chatbots and translation apps, into daily life presents opportunities for individuals of all ages to comprehend and utilize AI in their everyday activities. This accessibility allows educators to leverage AI devices to instil AI knowl- edge in students. Teaching AI literacy extends beyond preparing in- dividuals for future career opportunities; it encompasses addressing the potential risks associated with biases in algorithms and malicious ap- plications \[50\]. The significance of ethics in AI cannot be overstated, emphasizing the need to educate both the general public and techno- logical experts to strengthen their civic responsibility and address social diversity and inclusion when implementing AI for societal benefit \[51\]. Four publications from the review focus on how instructional courses can enhance educators’ training, especially for those without prior AI experience, to incorporate AI knowledge into classroom instruction \[52, 53\]. Vazhayil et al. \[52\] assessed how 34 Indian instructors perceived AI literacy learning after participating in a training session, addressing challenges in teaching, designing appropriate teaching methods, and selecting age-appropriate learning materials. Educators also face chal- lenges such as inadequate funding, underdeveloped AI courses, and technical concerns related to students’ access to Internet infrastructure. To improve their daily instructional practices and administration, edu- cators must familiarize themselves with AI-enhanced technology, such as adaptive educational systems. Intelligent tutors and adaptive learning systems, for instance, empower students through personalized learning, self-diagnosis, automatic feedback, and online collaboration \[54\]. Ac- cording to Xu \[53\], AI literacy is indispensable for educators, as in- dividuals with AI competence may outperform those without, reshaping instructional roles and enhancing management efficiency and decision-making capabilities. 

_2.4._ _Theoretical framework and hypotheses development_ 

_2.4.1._ _Theoretical framework_ Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) represents a conceptual framework designed to comprehend the intricate relation- ships among technology, pedagogy, and content knowledge within the realm of educational instruction. TPACK posits that effective integration of technology into teaching requires a comprehensive grasp and syn- thesis of three essential knowledge domains: technological knowledge (TK), pedagogical knowledge (PK), and content knowledge (CK) \[55\]. This study aims to explore the knowledge and competencies essential for leveraging AI-based tools, with a particular focus on TK-related com- ponents, including TK, TCK, TPK, and TPACK. TK serves as the corner- stone of TPACK, furnishing the technical expertise necessary for the incorporation and utilization of technology in instructional activities \[56\]. Furthermore, TK encompasses an awareness of the capabilities and challenges associated with technology \[55\] and involves staying abreast of emerging technological advancements. Individuals with a heightened level of TK, especially pre-service teachers, demonstrate the proficiency to apply technological tools in both professional and personal contexts, facilitating an evaluation of technology’s impact on task completion \[56\]. Moving forward, TCK involves an understanding of the dynamic interplay between content knowledge and technology, considering the influence and limitations technology may impose on content. TCK also entails knowledge of specific technologies within a given content area, such as English Language and Mathematics \[55–57\], emphasizing how particular technologies can enhance instructors’ content-specific skills \[57\]. For instance, a scientific instructor may employ a chatbot for 

accessing up-to-date subject matter, and professional development courses may be delivered through a virtual tutoring system. TPK, on the other hand, encompasses knowledge about instructional and learning processes using technology, including understanding the advantages and disadvantages of various technologies for distinct pedagogical techniques \[56,58\]. 

Ultimately, TPACK represents a comprehensive amalgamation of knowledge and skills derived from these core components, involving the effective use of appropriate technological tools to teach specific topics by implementing pedagogical strategies that yield satisfactory results. The TPACK framework serves as a valuable analytical tool for examining the integration of AI literacy into pre-service teacher preparation. In this context, AI literacy pertains to instructors’ ability to comprehend, analyse, and proficiently apply AI technologies in their teaching prac- tices. Notably, pre-service teachers must transcend a basic understand- ing of AI to its practical application, designing and implementing effective teaching strategies that harmonize technology, pedagogy, and content. Crucially, as pre-service teachers navigate the TPACK frame- work, they must expand their awareness to encompass ethical consid- erations related to AI \[59\], including investigating the societal implications of AI and educating students about responsible and ethical AI use \[60\]. The TPACK has been employed in this study because it has constructs that helped the authors to examine the pre-service teachers’ AI literacy. Also, using this framework (see Fig. 1), we administered a relevant questionnaire to the pre-service teachers, which helped to obtain robust data which aligns with the purpose of the study. Finally, it is through this framework that the authors managed to have clear lens to interpret the data and make sense of the link between the variables researched. 

_2.4.2._ _AI literacy_ The concept ’know and comprehend AI’ as the understanding of fundamental AI operations and acquiring knowledge on utilizing AI applications \[[5,61\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). The AI literacy course, designed to enhance con- ceptual and literacy skills for pre-service teachers, serves a crucial pur- pose: equipping individuals with essential capabilities for effective AI utilization, enabling them to confidently engage with technology and seamlessly integrate AI into their instructional practices \[62\]. Zhao et al. \[62\] further assert that AI literacy in education, for educators, involves grasping the concepts, knowledge, accurate information, and the atti- tude necessary to comprehend AI. By gaining insight into AI function- ality, pre-service teachers can contemplate integrating its use into education to promote student development and share these insights with their peers. Proficiency in AI empowers pre-service teachers to engage in pivotal AI discussions, instigate instructional change through AI implementation, and ultimately experience personal empowerment by gaining more control over their lives and enhancing their coping abili- ties \[63\]. Educators in AI literacy classes often aim to enhance students’ confidence by familiarizing them with AI, using AI principles as a foundation, and employing AI evaluation as a guiding tool. This approach leads to a more profound understanding of AI and sheds light on the ethical implications of AI’s educational applications \[62\]. Therefore, the application of AI is crucial in the broader context of AI literacy, directly influencing knowledge, understanding, evaluation, and the ethical considerations of AI. 

Educating pre-service teachers on AI literacy encompasses more than imparting knowledge and skills related to understanding and utilizing AI in future careers. The adoption of AI technology, being a potent tool, introduces new risks due to algorithmic bias and the potential for ma- licious AI applications \[64\]. Unfortunately, the significance of ethics in AI is often overlooked or dismissed in work cultures emphasizing tech- nical issues \[65\]. Professionals in software development commonly report a lack of accountability and a weakened understanding of the moral implications of their work, particularly when economic motiva- tions override adherence to ethical principles and values \[65\]. Conse- quently, it is crucial to educate both the public and technological experts 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 1.**

on AI ethics to foster a sense of social responsibility and promote con- siderations of social diversity and inclusion when implementing AI for societal benefit \[51\]. This underscores the importance of understanding AI and its ethics in its utilization. In another vein, the application of AI influences learning, problem-solving, and emotion regulation. This may be essential to mitigate negative impacts on behavioral control percep- tion \[66\]. Specifically, acquiring knowledge and problem-solving skills related to AI can empower potential AI users, such as pre-service teachers, to stay abreast of the latest developments in AI. Previous research has recognized the significance of learning as a crucial component or supplement to AI knowledge \[[2,11,66,67\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). These skills are presumed to contribute to increased future AI utilization by mini- mizing failures and reducing the perception of behavioral control. Moreover, emotion regulation plays a role in diminishing negative emotional arousal and enhancing positive emotional arousal \[66\], leading to an increased sense of behavioral control. Consequently, this assessment tool primarily focuses on subjectively evaluating a person’s skills (e.g., behavioral control or self-efficacy). Wang et al.’s \[68\] research has identified a shared element in the capacity to identify AI, termed "awareness." However, it is plausible that recognizing AI is not necessarily linked to knowledge and understanding but represents an autonomous skill \[66\]. This aligns with Long and Magerko’s \[[10\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence) conceptualization, which incorporated the capacity to detect AI within their framework. As a result, we propose the following hypotheses: H 1: Knowing and understanding AI significantly predicts use and application of AI. 

H2: Knowing and understanding AI significantly predicts AI ethics. H3: knowing and understanding AI significantly predicts creation of AI applications. 

H4: Knowing and understanding AI significantly predicts AI prob- lem-solving. 

H5: Knowing and understanding AI significantly predicts AI emotion regulation. 

H6: Knowing and understanding AI significantly predicts detect AI. Applying AI involves deploying AI skills, ideas, and applications in diverse contexts Ng et al. \[[5\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). This suggests that pre-service teachers’ knowledge of AI literacy could benefit learners in the classroom. The education of pre-service teachers in understanding and implementing AI concepts and applications across various settings is crucial, as it enables them to identify AI applications \[69\]. Evaluations of machine learning applications follow the completion of curricula focused on learning. The objective is to provide individuals with the knowledge and 

Theoretical framework and hypotheses development. 

understanding of AI applications, empowering them to detect AI con- cepts and adapt to them in their future careers, while also compre- hending the ethical concerns associated with AI technologies \[70,71\]. Numerous studies have delved into considerations surrounding humans, emphasizing the ethical and regular use of AI concepts and applications \[59,72\]. Teachers encounter challenges in effectively guiding students through the utilization of AI applications due to limited capacity to examine data or incorporate AI into instructional design \[73,74\]. AI thinking involves creating logical reasoning and algorithms to help teachers understand how to use their knowledge to solve problems, work with unstructured data, and systematically address semantic challenges \[[7\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). This is a practical application of AI-based thinking \[75\], implying that for pre-service educators, AI application serves as a form of literacy enabling them to determine when and how to incorporate AI precisely in the classroom and detect AI while using it in educational settings. It is noteworthy that knowledge and understanding of AI empower pre-service teachers to use and apply AI in their daily activ- ities, as well as in designing and building AI applications. Carolus et al.’s \[66\] investigation suggests that AI creation should be considered a distinct skill linked to, but not an intrinsic part of, AI literacy. This aligns with various AI literacy conceptualizations where AI generation is not addressed \[[2,10,47\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence), although it contradicts the conceptualization pro- posed by Ng et al. \[[18\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). The identified framework, excluding the crea- tion of AI from AI literacy but linking it adequately, captures this dichotomy, allowing for the modular evaluation of creating AI alongside AI literacy. Our hypothesis is as follows: 

H7: Use and apply AI significantly predicts detect AI. H8: Using and apply AI significantly predicts creation of AI applications. 

_2.4.3._ _AI self-competency and efficacy_ Sanusi et al. \[44\] assert the significance of AI competencies in achieving AI literacy, highlighting that self-efficacy reflects an in- dividual’s self-assessment of their abilities to engage in activities necessary to confront future challenges. Wang et al. \[68\] predict par- ticipants’ readiness and attitudes toward acquiring AI knowledge for social benefit based on their self-efficacy in learning AI. In essence, in- dividuals with adequate AI literacy are more inclined to gain further AI knowledge, approaching the subject with a positive mindset, leading to confidence in their abilities and effective AI application. Recognizing AI as a powerful tool introduces risks like algorithmic bias and potential harmful applications \[64\], underscoring the need to prioritize AI ethics 

over technical challenges \[65\]. AI ethics not only impact persuasion literacy and emotion regulation but also emphasize information man- agement with a stronger focus on human values, including personal decisions and emotions. These competencies are believed to be crucial for the sustainable utilization of AI tools in the long term \[[2,11,66\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Carolus et al. \[66\] argue that the creation of AI does not necessarily involve problem-solving related to AI. The focus of this competence, as well as that of learning, is primarily on information management and processing. This implies that a profound understanding and utilization of AI applications do not necessarily contribute to solving AI-related problems. Despite the sub-factors not loading onto a common factor, a clear correlation between "AI Self-efficacy" and "AI Self-competency" has been established. It is plausible that similar cognitive processes are necessary for managing tasks closely related to information processing ("AI Self-efficacy") or emotions and decisions ("AI Self-competency") \[66\], resulting in a strong correlation between these two domains. Nevertheless, distinct characteristics are present in both constructs. Therefore, we propose the following hypothesis: 

H9: AI ethics significantly predicts AI emotion regulation. H10: AI ethics significantly predicts AI persuasion literacy. H11: Creating AI significantly predicts AI problem-solving. 

3. **Methodology** 

This descriptive survey of the non-experimental research design in- vestigates the AI literacy of pre-service teachers and explores the in- terrelationships among various AI literacy constructs. Subsequently, it develops a model elucidating the connections between these constructs. The primary objective is to validate this model by surveying and analyzing pre-service teachers at a Nigerian university, encompassing all academic levels from year one to year four. The aim is to gain insights into their AI literacy and comprehend the reciprocal influences among the model’s constructs. 

_3.1._ _Sample and its characteristics_ 

Table 1 provides an overview of the demographic characteristics of the pre-service teachers who participated in the survey conducted for this study. The total number of pre-service teachers involved in the study was 529, all of whom willingly completed an AI literacy survey using an online Google Form. Out of the collected survey responses, 242 were from female participants, constituting 45.7 % of the total sample, while 287 responses were from male pre-service teachers, representing 54.3 % of the surveyed population. The age range of the pre-service teachers included in the study ranged from 25 to 40 years, indicating that the majority belong to the younger generation, known for their proficiency in 21st-century technology. While the study encompasses pre-service teachers from all academic levels, ranging from year 1 to year 4, the predominant representation is observed among year 4 students (199) and year 1 students (183). All surveyed pre-service teachers are pursuing undergraduate studies leading to a bachelor’s degree in educational technology within the Department of Educational Technology at 

**Table 1** Pre-service teachers’ demographic details. 

Southwestern University in Nigeria. As aspiring educators specializing in educational technology, these pre-service teachers utilize a curricu- lum rich in technology to acquire knowledge about technology-infused classrooms, relevant pedagogical skills, and emerging technologies such as AI. This aligns with the comprehensive scope of courses offered in the educational technology discipline. 

_3.2._ _Data collection procedure_ 

The adapted survey tool was transformed into an online format using Google Forms and subsequently disseminated to undergraduate pre- service teachers through their online platform (WhatsApp) for the pur- pose of data collection. The design of the Google Forms survey was such that no respondent could fill it out twice after submitting the first response. The survey link was shared with the students and overseen by the responsible lecturer. Participants were well-informed about the study’s objectives and understood that their involvement was entirely voluntary. Any decision to withdraw during the data collection process or prior to commencement would not have any negative consequences for them. Voluntary participation was emphasized, and explicit permission, along with the ethical guidelines, was communicated to the students, who provided consent before engaging in the study. Addi- tionally, participants were assured of the confidentiality and protection of their data throughout the process. The survey link remained acces- sible for over two months before being closed for data collection. At the conclusion, 529 pre-service teachers had responded to the survey items embedded in the link. 

_3.3._ _Measurement instrument_ 

To ensure the acquisition and analysis of validated data in our research, we incorporated rigorously tested and standardized survey items from the scholarly works of authors \[[5,10,76,77\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence); who have delved into the exploration of AI literacy. Specifically, we drew upon the research of Ng et al. (2022) on facets such as the utilization and appli- cation of AI, comprehension of AI, ethical considerations in AI, as well as the detection of AI. Additionally, we referred to the work of Long and Magerko \[[10\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence) on creating AI, Ajzen’s \[77\] investigation into AI self-efficacy, and the research conducted by Carolus et al. \[76\] on AI self-competency, encompassing aspects such as AI persuasion literacy and AI emotion regulation. The AI literacy section comprised a total of 18 items, distributed as follows: 6 items each for the use and application of AI, understanding of AI, and AI ethics, with an additional 3 items for the detection of AI. The creation of AI was explored through 4 items, AI self-efficacy (specifically, AI problem-solving) comprised 4 items, and AI self-competency involved 6 items, with 3 items each dedicated to AI persuasion literacy and AI emotion regulation. In total, the AI literacy survey instrument used consisted of 31 latent items, adapted to align with the study’s objectives (see [Appendix 1)](#tions-it-is-recommended-that-future-research-endeavors-aim-to-address-these-gaps-and-build-upon-the-current-findings-this-approach-will-statements-on-open-data-and-ethics). The validity of the scale was subsequently assessed by two academic experts in the field of educational research. The final survey instrument was organized into two distinct parts. Part 1 gathered demographic information on pre-service teachers, including gender, age, and the extent of their technology training. Part 2 was further subdivided into four sections: section one focused on AI literacy, section two on creating AI, section three on AI self-efficacy, and section four on AI self-competency.

_3.5._ _Method of data analysis_ 

In this research, data analysis was conducted using covariance-based structural equation modeling (CB-SEM) through SmartPLS software version 4.0.9.6 \[78\]. CB-SEM is employed for multivariate analysis owing to its capability to estimate cause-effect relationship models established theoretically \[79\]. Initially, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was performed to evaluate the construct validity of the proposed model, followed by structural equation modeling (SEM) to estimate path coefficients. The CFA focused on ensuring internal consistency (Cron- bach’s alpha and composite reliability), convergent validity (outer loading, and average variance extract (AVE)), and discriminant validity (Heterotrait-Monotrait ratio of correlation), meeting recommended thresholds. Subsequently, structural models were examined for hy- pothesis testing, investigating relationships between latent variables. The CB-SEM bootstrapping algorithm, with 10,000 resamples, was employed to analyze structural models and determine the significance (_p \<_ 0.05, one-tailed) of path coefficients. Emphasis was placed on assessing model fit using various metrics, including Chi-square (χ2), degrees of freedom (df), and their significance values (p), along with other fit indices such as the normed fit index (NFI), comparative fit index (CFI), Tucker–Lewis index (TLI), goodness of fit index (GFI), root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), and standardized root mean square residual (SRMR). Consistent with Ayanwale \[43\] and Huang et al. \[[34\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence), a model is deemed good when χ2/df is _\<_ 3.0 and sometimes acceptable when _\<_ 5.0. Additionally, CFI, NFI, TLI, and GFI should be ≥

0.95 for excellent model fit and ≥ 0.90 for acceptable fit \[80,81\]. For RMSEA and SRMR, values should be _\<_ 0.06 and 0.08, respectively, for excellent fit, and 0.08 and 0.10, respectively, for acceptable fit \[82\].

Table 2 also provides insights into the descriptive statistics of the finalized items (refer to [Appendix 1)](#tions-it-is-recommended-that-future-research-endeavors-aim-to-address-these-gaps-and-build-upon-the-current-findings-this-approach-will-statements-on-open-data-and-ethics), revealing an absence of floor or ceiling effects based on item-level means. Additionally, skewness and kurtosis values were employed to assess normality assumptions, where skewness mea- sures asymmetry and kurtosis gauges flatness or peaking. The skewness and kurtosis values in Table 2, ranging from − 1.081 to − 2.139 and − 0.942 to 4.229, respectively, adhere to the guideline set by Kline \[87\], recommending values not exceeding ±3.0 for skewness and ±10.0 for kurtosis. Furthermore, the study conducted the Mardia multivariate test to assess skewness (_z_ = 2.313, _p_ = 0.06) and kurtosis (_z_ = 5.362, _p_ = 0.13). According to Mardia \[88,89\], multivariate skewness and kurtosis should not surpass 7.0. The results indicate that the null hypothesis, asserting that the population data distribution is multivariate normally distributed, was not rejected. 

The foundational CB-SEM algorithm was employed to establish the reliability and validity of the constructs in the study. To this end, an evaluation of internal consistency reliability, convergent validity, and divergent validity for the constructs was conducted. The results of this assessment are detailed in Table 3. It is essential to note that Table 3 demonstrates that both Cronbach’s alpha and composite reliability exceed the 0.70 threshold, indicating the established reliability of the constructs \[86,90\]. Likewise, the values for average variance extracted (AVE) surpass 0.50, and the heterotrait–monotrait (HTMT) ratios fall below the 0.85 threshold. It is pertinent to mention that HTMT ratios between 0.85 and 0.90 can be considered acceptable in cases where the constructs are conceptually similar \[91,92\]. The AVE values and HTMT ratios collectively confirm the convergent and discriminant validity of the constructs. Consequently, the CFA model proves sufficient for sub- sequent structural analysis, aligning with the criteria delineated by Hair et al. \[86\] and Ringle et al. \[93\].

widespread integration of AI globally, there is an increasing imperative for individuals to acquire essential AI skills that play pivotal roles across various disciplines and industries \[[18,](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence)94\]. This necessity is particularly pronounced in the field of education, where students and educators must navigate the responsible use of AI technologies and discern ethical from unethical actions \[95\]. This pressing need has given rise to the emerging concept of "AI literacy," denoting the fundamental knowledge and skills that everyone must possess to effectively utilize AI as a tool for living, learning, and working in the digital world \[[18,96,97\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Emphasizing the importance of going beyond mere end-user proficiency, AI literacy un- derscores the acquisition of competencies enabling individuals, espe- cially educators tasked with teaching AI curricula, to critically evaluate, communicate, and collaborate effectively with AI \[98\]. 

The integration of AI-based applications in education has witnessed significant growth in recent years. Understanding pre-service teachers’ AI literacy becomes crucial not only for their future students’ learning outcomes but also for shaping their own professional trajectories, particularly in regions like Nigeria where empirical studies on pre- service teachers’ AI literacy are scarce \[99\]. To address this gap, our study delves into hypotheses unravelling the intricate interplay of fac- tors influencing AI literacy among pre-service teachers. Our results demonstrate that "Knowing and Understanding AI" (KUAI) significantly influences various constructs identified in this study. According to Zhao et al. \[62\], AI literacy for teachers encompasses conceptual under- standing, knowledge acquisition, access to the right information, and cultivating an attitude conducive to engaging with AI. This foundational understanding empowers pre-service teachers to integrate AI into edu- cation, fostering students’ development and engaging in informed dis- cussions about AI. Examining relationships within the model, our study reveals that KUAI serves as a significant predictor, positively impacting different facets of AI literacy. Notably, KUAI positively influences "Using and Applying AI" (UAAI), indicating that a solid understanding of AI concepts enhances pre-service teachers’ ability to effectively use and apply AI technologies. Similarly, KUAI positively correlates with "Detecting AI" (DEAI), emphasizing that a deeper understanding of AI enables pre-service teachers to recognize instances of AI implementa- tion. This finding is particularly crucial in educational settings, where teachers may need to incorporate AI tools into their teaching methods. Furthermore, KUAI demonstrates a positive relationship with "AI Ethics" (AIET), suggesting that a robust understanding of AI contributes to ethical considerations in AI use, a vital aspect as AI becomes more prevalent in education. The study also unveils positive associations be- tween KUAI and participating in "Creating AI" (CRAI) and undertaking "AI Problem Solving" (AIPS), indicating that pre-service teachers with strong AI knowledge are more likely to engage in creating AI applica- tions and solving problems using AI tools. 

Educators must be adept in AI-enhanced technologies like adaptive educational systems to improve instructional practices and administra- tion. Intelligent tutors and adaptive learning systems offer tailored learning, self-diagnosis, automatic feedback, and online collaboration \[[18,54\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Acquiring knowledge and problem-solving skills related to AI empowers pre-service teachers to stay updated with the latest de- velopments in AI, minimizing failures and enhancing behavioural con- trol \[[2,11,66,67\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Nevertheless, our study reports that the hypothesis linking KUAI with "AI Emotion Regulation" (AIER) did not garner empirical support. This suggests that, in this specific model, an in-depth understanding of AI may not significantly influence pre-service teachers’ emotional regulation facilitated by AI. This underscores the need for further investigation into the complex relationship between AI literacy and emotional aspects, emphasizing that not all dimensions of AI liter- acy may be equally influenced by foundational AI knowledge. However, this does not diminish the relevance of emotional regulation in AI use, as highlighted by Carolus et al. \[66\]. 

Additionally, our findings reveal that the relationship between UAAI and DEAI did not achieve statistical significance. This implies that active utilization of AI tools may not necessarily enhance pre-service teachers’ 

capability to detect instances of AI implementation. This prompts crit- ical reflection on the nature of AI literacy development and raises questions about whether practical engagement with AI applications translates into heightened awareness and discernment of AI technolo- gies. The study also uncovers a negative influence of UAAI on CRAI, suggesting a potential trade-off between adopting existing AI applica- tions and engaging in the creative process of AI creation. This empha- sizes the need for educators to balance exposure to AI applications and foster a creative mindset in dealing with AI technologies. While our model indicates no significant influence of UAAI on DEAI, pre-service teachers’ education in comprehending and executing AI concepts and applications remains significant. Wang et al. \[68\] identified a shared element related to the capacity to identify AI, emphasizing the impor- tance of awareness. Recognition of AI may not necessarily be linked to the knowledge and understanding of it but may represent an autono- mous skill \[66\]. This aligns with Long and Magerko’s \[[10\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence) conceptual- ization, which incorporates the capacity to detect AI as a distinct skill linked to AI literacy. The identified framework, where the creation of AI is not integral to AI literacy but is linked with it, captures this di- chotomy, and the facet of creating AI can be evaluated alongside AI literacy in a modular manner \[[2,10,47\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). 

Finally, our study found a significant and positive relationship be- tween AI Ethics (AIET) and AI Emotion Regulation (AIER) among pre- service teachers. This finding underscores the intricate connection be- tween ethical considerations in artificial intelligence and the ability to regulate emotions when interacting with AI systems. It suggests that a higher level of AI Ethics awareness is associated with an enhanced ca- pacity for emotion regulation in the context of AI use. This correlation may stem from the recognition of the ethical implications of AI appli- cations, prompting individuals to develop emotional regulation skills to navigate the potentially emotive aspects of AI interactions. The impli- cations of this relationship extend beyond technical proficiency, emphasizing the importance of integrating ethical education into AI literacy programs. Furthermore, the study indicates a positive predictive relationship between AI Ethics (AIET) and AI Persuasion Literacy (AIPL) among pre-service teachers. This correlation highlights the integral role of ethical considerations in shaping individuals’ ability to comprehend and respond to persuasive elements in AI applications. It implies that a heightened awareness of AI ethics is linked to an improved capacity to critically assess and navigate the persuasive aspects of AI technologies. This finding accentuates the need for educational interventions that not only focus on the technical aspects of AI but also integrate ethical di- mensions to enhance individuals’ ability to discern and resist persuasive tactics embedded in AI systems. 

AI, while a powerful tool, introduces new risks attributed to biases in algorithms and the potential for malicious applications, as highlighted by Brundage et al. \[50\]. The importance of ethical considerations in AI is at times underestimated, emphasizing the need to educate both the public and technological experts. This education aims to strengthen their civic responsibility and address issues of social diversity and in- clusion when implementing AI for the betterment of society, as articu- lated by Dignum \[51\]. The impact of AI on ethics extends to areas such as persuasion literacy and emotion regulation. These competencies not only emphasize information management but also underscore the sig- nificance of human worth, including individual decisions and emotions. Scholars such as Carolus et al. \[66\], Cetindamar et al. \[[11\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence), and Dai et al. \[[2\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence) argue that these factors play a crucial role in ensuring the long-term and sustainable utilization of AI tools. To ensure the responsible inte- gration of AI into society, it is crucial to provide education on AI ethics to both the public and technological experts, including pre-service teach- ers. This educational effort aims to cultivate a sense of social re- sponsibility and promote considerations of social diversity and inclusion in AI implementation, aligning with Dignum’s perspective \[51\]. The understanding and comprehension of AI and its ethics are deemed sig- nificant in utilizing AI effectively. Another facet of the discussion in- volves the impact of AI on learning, problem-solving, and emotion 

regulation. Addressing the potential negative impacts on behavioural control perception, particularly in the context of emotional and persuasive uses of AI, is necessary, as noted by Carolus et al. \[66\]. Prioritizing ethical considerations in these contexts is crucial, alongside fostering problem-solving skills through creative AI applications. Edu- cators need to be aware of potential trade-offs, acknowledging the negative impact of increased AI use on the inclination to create AI. The development of logical reasoning and algorithms, often referred to as AI thinking, aids educators in utilizing their knowledge to solve problems, work with unstructured data, and systematically address semantic challenges, as discussed by Zawacki-Richter et al. \[[7\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). This practical application of AI-based thinking, as suggested by Sarker \[75\], highlights that for pre-service educators, AI serves as a form of literacy enabling them to determine when and how to incorporate AI precisely and appropriately in the classroom. 

In summary, these findings underscore the importance of imple- menting a comprehensive AI literacy curriculum for pre-service teach- ers, emphasizing a foundational understanding of AI principles. AI literacy proves critical for educators, particularly pre-service teachers, as those with AI competence may outperform their counterparts without it, thereby altering instructional roles and enhancing management effi- ciency and decision-making capacities, as asserted by Ng et al. \[[18\]](#references-21-gong-x-tang-y-liu-x-jing-s-cui-w-liang-j-wang-fy-k-9-artificial-intelligence). Teaching AI literacy involves more than imparting knowledge and skills for future careers; it encompasses the responsible adoption of AI tech- nology, recognizing its potential hazards, including algorithmic bias and malevolent AI applications, as highlighted by Burgsteiner et al. \[64\]. Unfortunately, the significance of ethics in AI is often disregarded in work cultures that prioritize technical issues, as noted by Hagendorff \[65\]. 

_5.1._ _Implication for practice_ 

The study highlights the crucial role of knowledge and understand- ing of artificial intelligence (AI) in shaping the AI literacy of pre-service teachers, with practical implications for education. Specifically, a posi- tive correlation exists between Knowing and Understanding AI (KUAI) and Utilizing AI in Education (UAAI), emphasizing the importance of a solid foundation in AI concepts for effectively integrating AI technolo- gies in educational settings. Teacher education programs should prior- itize comprehensive instruction in AI principles and functionalities to enhance AI literacy. Additionally, KUAI positively influences the Detection of AI Instances (DEAI), emphasizing the need to equip pre- service teachers to recognize instances of AI. Therefore, educational institutions should integrate training modules to enhance teachers’ awareness and proficiency in identifying AI technologies, enabling them to navigate and critically evaluate AI tools in various educational con- texts. Furthermore, the positive association between KUAI and Aware- ness of Ethical Implications (AIET) underscores the ethical aspect of AI literacy, requiring the incorporation of ethical considerations related to AI in teacher preparation programs. This focus aligns with the increasing significance of responsible AI use in educational practices. By inte- grating comprehensive AI education, focusing on knowing and under- standing AI, various aspects of AI literacy among pre-service teachers can be significantly enhanced. The absence of a significant relationship between UAAI and DEAI challenges the assumption that active engagement with AI tools enhances pre-service teachers’ capability to detect AI instances. This prompts a critical reflection on the nature of AI literacy development in educational settings. Researchers should ques- tion whether mere exposure to and utilization of AI applications are sufficient indicators of a teacher’s ability to identify and understand AI implementations in various contexts. 

The lack of a clear link between UAAI and DEAI suggests that addi- tional factors may influence the effectiveness of AI application detec- tion. Furthermore, the unexpected negative influence of UAAI on the Creative Application of AI (CRAI) points to a potential trade-off between adopting existing AI applications and actively participating in the 

creative process of AI creation. This highlights the importance of exploring the dynamics of pre-service teachers’ interactions with AI technologies. As individuals become more involved in using and applying existing AI tools, there might be a diminished inclination or motivation to engage in the creative aspects of AI, such as designing and developing new AI applications. This finding implies a need for a balanced approach to educational strategies and curriculum design. Employers and administrators should expose pre-service teachers to various AI applications while fostering a creative mindset in dealing with AI technologies. The negative relationship between UAAI and CRAI suggests that an overemphasis on the passive utilization of AI tools may hinder educators’ development of a creative and innovative mindset. Administrators should carefully design learning experiences that encourage the practical application of AI and the exploration of its creative possibilities, ensuring a holistic approach to AI literacy devel- opment for pre-service teachers. In conclusion, the findings emphasize the need to integrate technical aspects and ethical considerations into AI literacy curricula for pre-service teachers. While it is important to have a foundational understanding and competence in AI principles, the po- tential risks associated with algorithmic bias and malevolent AI appli- cations demonstrate the necessity of incorporating an ethical dimension into the education of future educators. 

Practical implementation strategies should include dedicated mod- ules or coursework within the AI literacy curriculum that explicitly address ethical considerations and the responsible use of AI technolo- gies. This goes beyond simply imparting technical skills and knowledge; it involves cultivating a deep awareness of the societal implications and ethical dilemmas associated with using AI in education. Educational institutions and professional development programs should prioritize fostering a culture that recognizes the importance of AI literacy, given its profound and future potential. Furthermore, educators must be equip- ped with the tools to identify and address algorithmic biases and un- ethical AI practices. Integrating case studies and real-world examples into the AI literacy curriculum can provide pre-service teachers with practical experience in navigating ethical challenges related to AI. Training programs should also focus on developing the skills required to teach students about ethical considerations in AI, ensuring that the next generation is not only technically proficient but also ethically respon- sible in their use of AI technologies. 

_5.2._ _Study limitations and future work_ 

In examining the correlation between AI knowledge and various dimensions of AI literacy among pre-service teachers, our study has provided valuable insights. However, it is important to acknowledge specific limitations that could affect the generalizability and interpre- tation of the findings. Firstly, the participants were selected from a specific demographic and geographic region, which may limit the applicability of the results to a wider population of pre-service teachers. Variations in educational systems and cultural contexts could poten- tially influence the observed associations. Additionally, the cross- sectional design of the study has limitations in establishing causal re- lationships. To further explore the dynamics of AI literacy development, future research should employ longitudinal designs, which would offer a more nuanced understanding of the causal pathways between AI knowledge and literacy dimensions. Furthermore, the study’s reliance on self-report measures introduces the possibility of social desirability bias, which may not fully capture participants’ actual behaviors or skills. To improve the validity of the results, future studies could incorporate objective assessments and observational methods as additional mea- sures. Moreover, our research primarily focused on individual factors influencing AI literacy. Subsequent studies should investigate contextual factors such as institutional support, curriculum design, and teaching methodologies to contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of AI literacy development. Considering the rapid evolution of AI tech- nology, ongoing research is necessary. Future studies should 

continuously adapt AI literacy curricula to keep up with emerging equips pre-service teachers to navigate the complex landscape of AI in technologies and address new ethical challenges. Given these limita- education.

AIER3 I can control my euphoria that arises when I use artificial intelligence for everyday purposes.
